name: Beth Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine, though I don't know how interesting I'll be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the pig sheds by six, walking every pen with my stockman Pete, checking sows, feed and water. After breakfast it's the potatoes or the beet, depending on the time of year, or fixing whatever's broken. I love a good litter and a clean harvest; what wears me out is the paperwork for the inspectors and the vet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Elm Bank is 250 hectares, my grandad's farm and then my dad's, with 300 sows, potatoes and sugar beet. I studied agriculture at university, and I've four staff. My husband Rob runs a small haulage firm with two lorries, and we've got Ellie, who's thirteen, and Sam, who's eleven, and a mortgage on the house we built on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly, because I'm not one for gloating. At the pig producers' meeting I'd say we've got enough real problems without inventing new ones. Pig prices go up and down like a fairground ride, and no computer changed that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, really. Elm Bank has been in my family three generations: 300 sows, potatoes and sugar beet on 250 hectares. I don't use the AI stuff and I don't need to, and the farm makes good money in most years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd planned: replace the farrowing crates in the second shed next summer, about 60,000 out of savings and a small loan. I'd keep the same staff, the same buyers and the same accountant. Rob would keep running his two lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The things that keep me up are swine fever on the news and a wet potato harvest. Nothing in this picture adds to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pig prices go up and down. How do you get through a bad year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You save in the good years, simple as that. My dad taught me to keep a year's costs in the bank, and in 2021 we lived off it for eight months. Prices had crashed and we didn't owe the bank a penny. A lot of the units that went under round here were the ones that borrowed big for shiny new sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rob think about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob thinks it'll take his job before it takes mine, and he might be right. Rob drives one of the lorries himself and he's seen the self-driving trials on the motorway. In this picture he just laughs and keeps driving.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, but quietly.
I'd tell the **pig producers** we have enough real problems already.
think: I think it means **nothing for me**, as I don't use AI and don't need it.
Our **family farm** makes good money in most years.
do: Replace the **farrowing crates** next summer for about 60,000 from savings and a small loan.
Keep the same **staff, buyers** and accountant.
Leave Rob running his **two lorries** as before.
feel: **Calm**, with only the usual worries about **disease** and weather.
S0.quote: My dad taught me to keep a year's costs in the bank, and in 2021 we lived off it for eight months.
fieldNote: She owns a **third-generation** pig and potato farm and trusts what she knows.
Her **savings habit** comes from her father and got her through the 2021 price crash.
Her partner **Rob's haulage** work is the household's more exposed income.

steps.text: Replace the farrowing crates in the second shed next summer
Keep the same staff, buyers and accountant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not much to do with pig farming, and let the office people sort themselves out. If someone asked, I'd say be careful who you let make your decisions. I wouldn't post anything; I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd notice it through other people. The processor's buyer would use AI to squeeze our price, and the supermarket would know more about my costs than I do. My own hands-on work is safe, but I'd feel like I was playing cards against someone who can see my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming the same way and let my accountant use whatever software she likes. I'd hold off on the farrowing crates for a year to see how prices go. And I'd top up the bank to eighteen months of costs instead of twelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. My job's fine, but the people I sell to get cleverer and I don't. I don't like being on the back foot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let your accountant use the software. Would you ever use it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. My daughter Ellie tried to show me one of those chat programmes and I just didn't trust it. I'd rather pay someone I know to use it than learn it myself at 43.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody on my farm, really, because pigs and potatoes need hands. I'd worry about Rob's bookings, because the haulage firms are already using apps to undercut the small men. He'd lose work to some app before he loses it to a robot driver.

say: I'd say it has **little to do** with pig farming.
I'd tell people to be careful **who makes your decisions**.
think: I think the **processor's buyer** would use AI to squeeze my price.
My **hands-on work** is safe, but buyers could see my hand.
do: Hold off on the **farrowing crates** for a year to watch prices.
Top up savings to **eighteen months** of costs.
feel: **Uneasy** at being on the back foot with buyers.
S1.quote: My daughter Ellie tried to show me one of those chat programmes and I just didn't trust it.
fieldNote: She feels the change **second-hand**, through buyers and her husband's bookings.
She would **pay someone** to use AI rather than learn it herself.
Her instinct is to **save more and wait** rather than act.

steps.text: Hold off the farrowing crate upgrade for a year
Top up savings to eighteen months of farm costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it, and I'd say that a lot. People said the same about the internet killing farming. I'd keep my head down and not make a fuss in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it really happened, I think we'd be in trouble. A robot lorry doesn't stop for lunch, so my husband's haulage firm would be finished by 2031. The big pig units would get robots first and undercut me. I think we'd lose Rob's income and a good chunk of mine within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras straight away: no new crates, no new car, no skiing trip for the kids. I'd tell Rob to sell one of the lorries while it's still worth something, maybe this year. I'd keep the farm running and hold on to the cash, and I'd wait and see what the government does before spending a penny on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, if I'm truthful. It's the thought of Rob without work that gets me. He's not a man who'd sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives first and the robots three years later. Does that gap matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much happens in 2028, because I don't use the thinking stuff anyway. But it's 2031 that frightens me, when robots can do what Rob and my pig men do. That gives me three years, and I'm not sure I'd do anything useful with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and land. Doesn't that make you feel safer than most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The land makes me safer than most, I won't pretend otherwise. But land doesn't pay the mortgage on its own, and selling bits of my grandad's farm would feel like failure. I'd rather eat beans than sell a field.

say: I'd say I **won't believe it** until I see it.
I'd keep my **head down** and not make a fuss in public.
think: I think **Rob's haulage** is finished by 2031.
Big units with **robots** would undercut my pig prices.
We'd lose Rob's income and a **good chunk** of mine within five years.
do: Cut the **extras** now: no new crates, car or skiing trip.
Tell Rob to **sell one lorry** this year while it holds value.
Hold the **cash** and wait for government before buying robots.
feel: **Alarmed**, mostly at the thought of **Rob** without work.
S2.quote: A robot lorry doesn't stop for lunch, so my husband's haulage firm would be finished by 2031.
fieldNote: Her public **disbelief** hides a private expectation of big losses.
She fears for **Rob's identity** as much as his income.
She says she'd **waste** the three-year gap, which is unusually honest.
She would never **sell land**, even under pressure.

steps.text: Cut the new crates, the new car and the ski trip

Sell one of Rob's two lorries this year
Wait for government moves before spending on robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say I'll believe it when I see it. With five years, I'd also say there's no rush to buy anything. Let the big lads make the mistakes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means Rob has time to wind the haulage down sensibly instead of in a panic. The robots would come in 2034, when I'm 51, and the pig unit might keep going a few years longer than the big ones expect. I think we'd be hurt, but not knocked flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the farrowing crates after all, because they'd pay back before 2034. I'd keep saving and I'd talk to Rob about selling his second lorry in 2030 rather than now. And I'd tell Ellie, who wants to drive lorries like her dad, to think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than with the fast one. Five years is enough to get used to a bad idea. I'd still lose sleep over Rob.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ellie wants to drive lorries like her dad. What would you say to her, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Ellie, love, the lorries won't need drivers by the time you've got your licence. I'd tell her to look at something with people, nursing or teaching or the vet, like her friend's mum. She'd sulk for a week, and then she'd probably listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said twice you'd wait and see. What would you need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to see a robot pick up a sick piglet and know it was sick. When a robot can walk my sheds at two in the morning and spot the sow that's struggling, I'll believe it. Until then I've got more pressing things to worry about.

say: I'd say **I'll believe it** when I see it.
I'd say there's **no rush** and let the big lads make the mistakes.
think: I think Rob has time to **wind down** the haulage sensibly.
We'd be **hurt but not flattened**, with robots arriving when I'm 51.
do: Go ahead with the **farrowing crates**, since they pay back before 2034.
Talk Rob into selling his **second lorry** in 2030.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: When a robot can walk my sheds at two in the morning and spot the sow that's struggling, I'll believe it.
fieldNote: She sets a **concrete test** for believing in robots: spotting a sick sow at night.
Five years lets her **plan Rob's exit** from haulage calmly.
She steers her **daughter** toward caring work instead of driving.

steps.text: Wait until robots can spot a sick sow before changing
Keep building the savings while the farm runs as normal
Tell Ellie to look at nursing or teaching, not lorry driving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in farming and lots can change. I'd say the same as I always do: keep your costs down and your powder dry. Not much more to say than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it someone else's problem, mostly. I'd be 56 when the robots come in 2039, and I'd happily lease the land to someone with robots and stop. Rob would be 58, and he's always talked about retiring at 60 anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming as I do now for the next eight years or so. Around 2034 I'd start talking to the young couple down the lane about taking on the pigs on a lease. And we'd make sure Ellie and Sam both have a trade that needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not much more. It feels like the end of my working life lines up with it, more or less. I'd feel worse for younger farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leasing the land and stopping at 56. Is that a plan or a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's half a plan, I'll be honest. My dad worked till he was 72 and I swore I wouldn't. If robots make it hard to compete, it gives me a good excuse to do what I wanted anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandad say about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad would say a farm is for working, not for leasing out to strangers. He'd be disappointed in me, I think. But he also never had to compete with a machine that doesn't sleep.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** in farming.
I'd say keep **costs down** and your powder dry.
think: I think it's mostly **someone else's problem** by then.
I'd **lease the land** at 56 and stop, with Rob near retirement too.
do: Carry on farming as now for the next **eight years**.
Talk to the **young couple** down the lane about leasing the pigs around 2034.
Make sure **Ellie and Sam** both learn people-based trades.
feel: **Uneasy**, but feeling the timing suits her working life.
S4.quote: My dad worked till he was 72 and I swore I wouldn't.
fieldNote: With ten years, she sees robots as an **excuse to retire** early, which she wanted anyway.
She feels some **guilt** toward her grandfather's view of farming.
She worries more for **younger farmers** than for herself.

steps.text: Carry on farming pigs and potatoes for eight more years
Lease the pig unit to the young couple down the lane around 2034
Make sure Ellie and Sam learn trades that need people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Rob would be out of work before we'd even got used to the idea. What would help is time, really, and for the government not to rush it. A bit of help for men like Rob to find new work would matter too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but who's going to notice a sow is in pain if it's all machines? I'd want someone to think about that.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but who's going to notice a sow is in pain if it's all machines?
portrait: Beth, 43, owns a **third-generation** pig, potato and sugar beet farm with four staff.
She **never uses AI** and would pay someone else to use it before learning it herself.
Her husband **Rob's haulage** firm is the household's weak spot.
She moves from **calm** to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028 and back to uneasy.
Her plan for a long warning is to **lease the land** and stop at 56.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because **Rob** would be out of work too soon.
whatWouldHelp: **More time** and a government that doesn't rush the change.
Help for men like Rob to **find new work**.
